transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-02-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Jordan Kim (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Sunflare CTO), Marcus Li (Sunflare Head Eng), Ellen Park (Sunflare Security)

Auto-Summary (AI):
Sunflare is evaluating Redwood for a mix of low-latency user-facing features and high-throughput batch tasks. Primary constraints: monthly budget cap (~$25k), P95 latency target < 450ms for chat flows, and SOC2/compliance needs (KMS + audit logs). They want tradeoffs between hosted per-token pricing, dedicated reserved capacity, and private VPC for regulated logs. Next steps: pricing matrix, benchmarking pilot, send security pack.

Topics: per-token pricing, batching/caching levers, dedicated vs hosted costs, VPC/private, SOC2/KMS, pilot scope and success metrics.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Rivera: Hey everybody, thanks for joining — I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account, Jordan — our SE — is with me.
[00:10] Priya Desai: Hi Alex, hi Jordan. Thanks, we'll be brief. I'm Priya, CTO at Sunflare. Marcus and Ellen are on.
[00:15] Marcus Li: Hey.
[00:18] Ellen Park: Hi all.
[00:22] Jordan Kim: Great — quick agenda: understand your workload and constraints, talk about per-token math, batching and caching levers, and then sketch a pilot. Sound good?
[00:30] Priya Desai: Yup. Our use case split: 60% real-time chat (user query -> model -> UI), 40% nightly enrichment batch jobs. We have a hard budget cap of around $25k/mo for this project initially. Latency for the chat path needs to feel instant — p95 under 450ms ideally.
[00:45] Alex Rivera: Good to know. When you say tokens per request, ballpark?
[00:50] Marcus Li: Average prompt + response is about 450 tokens but it varies. Batch jobs produce longer contexts up to ~6k tokens.
[00:58] Jordan Kim: Ok that's helpful. For per-token math, there are three knobs: model selection (smaller vs larger), batching, and cache/prefix reuse. Hosted per-token pricing gives you on-demand with zero infra ops; dedicated is reserved GPU pools with lower per-token from better utilization but needs commit.
[01:20] Priya Desai: How big are the savings typically on dedicated?
[01:25] Jordan Kim: Depends on utilization. In our experience, at 60-70% sustained utilization, dedicated can be 30-50% cheaper per inference token versus hosted. But you need the commit and the right batching profile. If you can't reach those utilization levels, hosted sometimes wins.
[01:40] Ellen Park: Security question — on hosted, do you get KMS integration? Where do logs live?
[01:46] Alex Rivera: Hosted offers optional envelope encryption and we integrate with customer-managed KMS for key rotation; audit logs are retained in our control plane but we can export to your SIEM. If you need full data residency and VPC, that's where Private comes in — VPC peering or on-prem if required.
[02:02] Marcus Li: For our compliance team, exporting logs to our S3 with encryption-at-rest under our KMS is a hard requirement.
[02:08] Jordan Kim: We can set up cross-account log deliveries; we'll include the topology diagrams. There are some tradeoffs for latency with cross-account hops but typically negligible for chat workloads.
[02:18] Priya Desai: Walk me through an example per-token cost for our 450-token median.
[02:24] Jordan Kim: Sure. For hosted on a mid-sized model we might be at ~$0.8 per 1k tokens (prompt+completion combined), so a 450-token exchange is roughly $0.36 per call. If you do 100k chat calls/month that's $36k, which is above your 25k cap. But you can drop cost via batching for the batch pipeline and by using a smaller model for some intents, and caching prefixes for repeated system prompts.
[02:50] Marcus Li: Ok that's a red flag — $36k is over. How can batching help the real-time chat?
[02:56] Jordan Kim: For user-facing chat, batching is less helpful since you need low latency per user. But we do continuous micro-batching and dynamic batching that preserves p95 targets. More impactful for your nightly jobs; batching and KV cache re-use can cut per-token compute by 40-70% depending on sequence reuse.
[03:16] Priya Desai: You mentioned prefix caching — can you explain?
[03:20] Jordan Kim: Yeah — common startup context (system prompt + few-shot examples) can be cached as KV cache and reused across requests so you only compute the final tokens. For many chat flows that saves 30-60% of compute. Our platform supports automatic prefix/KV caching and will surface hit rates in the console.
[03:36] Ellen Park: Those caches live encrypted? If someone gets access to the cache, is it plaintext?
[03:40] Alex Rivera: Caches stored on the serving layer are encrypted at rest; keys are managed with KMS. For Private deployments, you control the KMS.
[03:46] Priya Desai: Back to pricing — you mentioned tiered hosted pricing — can we mix models? For example use hosted for spikes and dedicated baseline?
[03:54] Jordan Kim: Absolutely — smart routing lets you route traffic by policy. You can anchor baseline traffic on Dedicated and route spikes to Hosted, or route by latency/cost rules. That gives cost predictability while handling bursts without overprovisioning.
[04:10] Marcus Li: For Dedicated, what's the commitment structure? Monthly or yearly? And is burst capacity charged extra?
[04:16] Alex Rivera: Dedicated is typically reserved monthly or annual commits; we have flexible burst add-ons where you pay for consumed burst tokens or burst VMs. We'll show sample numbers in the pricing sheet.
[04:26] Priya Desai: The math seems sensitive to our QPS pattern — maybe we should do a pilot. What's a minimal pilot you recommend?
[04:34] Jordan Kim: A focused 2-week pilot: 1) run the chat workload on hosted to capture real token distribution & latency, 2) replay same workload on a small dedicated pool to compare p50/p95 and unit cost, 3) apply caching/quantization and measure delta. We typically provision a sandbox dedicated node for the pilot.
[04:52] Priya Desai: How much does the pilot cost?
[04:54] Alex Rivera: Pilots are usage-based; we can cap it. For budgeting, expect < $2k if traffic volumes are modest; Jordan will size it after you send traffic characteristics.
[05:03] Marcus Li: Our nightly batch uses sequence lengths up to 6k — any special notes for that?
[05:09] Jordan Kim: Long sequences favor models optimized for long context and can be accelerated with attention kernels and quantization. Also batching is more effective here. We might recommend quantized 8-bit or even 4-bit for batch jobs to save cost without visible quality loss. We'll include model variant suggestions.
[05:26] Ellen Park: From security side: SOC2, pen test reports, and whether Redwood supports SSO with SAML + SCIM for provisioning.
[05:34] Alex Rivera: We are SOC2 Type II certified; pen test summary is in our security pack. SSO via SAML + SCIM is supported with RBAC. We'll share the security dossier.
[05:44] Priya Desai: If we go Dedicated and host sensitive logs, where do audit logs land?
[05:49] Jordan Kim: With Dedicated, audit logs can be forwarded to your logging endpoint (S3/CloudWatch) under your KMS. The control plane still collects operational telemetry but we can limit retention and export.
[05:59] Priya Desai: Great. A couple of nitty-gritty: what's the expected p95 improvement on Dedicated vs Hosted for chat if we tune batching?
[06:06] Jordan Kim: For user-facing low-concurrency chat, p95 improvement might be modest — maybe 10-20% — since network and scheduling matter. But for sustained high throughput with good batching, dedicated lowers tail latency by reducing queueing and you get more predictable P95. We'll quantify in the pilot.
[06:22] Marcus Li: About model versions and rollouts — can we pin certain endpoints to model versions and fallback to smaller ones when overloaded?
[06:29] Alex Rivera: Yes — rollouts, canaries, and automatic fallback policies are supported. You can pin a route to a primary model and set fallback to a cheaper or smaller variant. That helps cost-control during spikes.
[06:40] Priya Desai: Okay timeline: we want pilot before end of Feb if possible. Is that realistic?
[06:46] Alex Rivera: Yes — if you send the sample traffic and token distribution this week, Jordan can size and we can start the pilot week of Feb 23.
[06:54] Priya Desai: I'll get that to you by tomorrow.
[06:58] Marcus Li: Do you have any tools to estimate cost ahead of time?
[07:02] Jordan Kim: We have an optimizer tool that simulates cost given token distribution and QPS; we'll run it as part of the pilot scoping. We'll also share a simple spreadsheet for quick eyeballing.
[07:12] Priya Desai: About quantization — any change in accuracy we should worry about?
[07:16] Jordan Kim: For many JSON/structured output tasks, int8/4 quantization is fine. For sensitive LLM tasks with nuanced reasoning, we recommend evaluating on your eval set. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles per model and workload.
[07:31] Ellen Park: One more question: retention policies for logs and model inputs — do you store customer prompts by default?
[07:36] Alex Rivera: By default, hosted stores short-term request logs for debugging; customers can opt-out of data retention or request prompt deletion. For Dedicated/Private, you can set retention policies and we support no-retention configs.
[07:47] Priya Desai: That's good. For the pilot success metrics, we'd expect: 1) cost per 1k tokens within x% of projection, 2) p95 under 450ms for chat, 3) KV cache hit rate above 20% for chat flows.
[07:59] Jordan Kim: Those are reasonable — we'll document them in the kickoff doc.
[08:05] Alex Rivera: Quick note on bursting: if you anchor on Dedicated and you've got a sudden sales spike, the routing can spill to hosted automatically but you'll pay hosted rates for that portion. That buys uptime and user experience.
[08:20] Marcus Li: Do you have any case studies with similar budget constraints?
[08:24] Alex Rivera: Yes, we have a fintech and a retail customer who used mixed hosting to keep costs in range; I'll include anonymized numbers.
[08:31] Priya Desai: Cool. Anything else on the roadmap features we should be aware of that affect cost?
[08:36] Jordan Kim: We're launching more advanced automatic batching heuristics and predictive KV prewarming which should improve cache hit rates for predictable workloads.
[08:44] Ellen Park: For the security pack, can you include the architecture for Private (VPC peering) and the on-prem option?
[08:50] Alex Rivera: Absolutely — we'll attach diagrams and the compliance attachments.
[08:55] Priya Desai: Ok thanks. Sounds like the pilot is the right next move.
[08:59] Alex Rivera: Great — recap of action items: Alex sends pricing + security pack; Jordan sizes pilot and config; Priya sends sample workload and constraint doc. We'll schedule the kickoff for week of Feb 23.
[09:12] Priya Desai: I'll send that today. Thanks everyone.
[09:15] Marcus Li: Thanks.
[09:17] Ellen Park: Thank you.
[09:20] Alex Rivera: Appreciate it. Chat soon.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional microphone overlap around 00:20-00:30, some technical terms auto-transcribed (e.g., KV cache -> K-V cash) and small proper noun confusions.
